title: Distributed Training: DDP, FSDP, DeepSpeed
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Distributed Training: DDP, FSDP, DeepSpeed ##### Eight GPUs, 1.9× the speed A team in Pune moved a fine-tuning job from one A100 to eight, expecting roughly eight times the throughput. They measured 1.9×. Their profile showed 61% of step time in `all_reduce`. The model was 1.3B parameters, they were using DDP with a microbatch of 2, and every single step synchronised 2.6 GB of gradients across eight GPUs over PCIe — not NVLink, because their cloud instance did not have it. Two changes fixed it. They raised the microbatch to 16 with gradient accumulation, so gradient synchronisation happened once per 8 microsteps instead of every one. And they enabled bucketed gradient overlap so communication happened *during* the backward pass rather than after it. 7.1× on eight GPUs. **Distributed training is a communication problem wearing a compute problem's clothes.** The arithmetic is embarrassingly parallel; the gradients are not. Understanding which strategy moves which bytes is what separates linear scaling from paying for idle GPUs. ##### The three axes of parallelism ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Model does not fit
or trains too slowly"] --> B{"Does one copy
fit on one GPU?"} B -->|Yes| C["DATA PARALLEL
replicate model,
split the batch"] B -->|No| D{"Do the weights
fit when sharded
across GPUs?"} D -->|Yes| E["FSDP / ZeRO-3
shard params, grads,
optimizer state"] D -->|No, single layer
too large| F["TENSOR PARALLEL
split individual
matrices"] D -->|No, too many
layers| G["PIPELINE PARALLEL
split layers
across GPUs"] C --> H["Combine as needed:
3D parallelism"] E --> H F --> H G --> H ``` | Strategy | Splits | Communication | Use when | |---|---|---|---| | **DDP** | Batch | All-reduce gradients | Model fits on one GPU | | **FSDP / ZeRO-3** | Params, grads, optim | All-gather + reduce-scatter | Model does not fit | | **Tensor parallel** | Individual matrices | All-reduce per layer | One layer too large; needs NVLink | | **Pipeline parallel** | Layers | Point-to-point activations | Many layers, slow interconnect | | **Sequence parallel** | Sequence dimension | All-to-all | Very long context | ##### DDP Every GPU holds a full model replica and processes a different slice of the batch. After the backward pass, gradients are averaged across all ranks with an all-reduce, so every replica applies an identical update. ```python import os import torch import torch.distributed as dist from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel as DDP from torch.utils.data.distributed import DistributedSampler def setup_ddp(): dist.init_process_group(backend="nccl") local_rank = int(os.environ["LOCAL_RANK"]) torch.cuda.set_device(local_rank) return local_rank, dist.get_rank(), dist.get_world_size() local_rank, rank, world_size = setup_ddp() model = build_model().to(local_rank) model = DDP( model, device_ids=[local_rank], gradient_as_bucket_view=True, # saves memory static_graph=True, # enables extra optimisations bucket_cap_mb=25, # overlap granularity ) sampler = DistributedSampler(dataset, num_replicas=world_size, rank=rank, shuffle=True, drop_last=True) loader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=micro_bs, sampler=sampler, num_workers=4, pin_memory=True, persistent_workers=True) for epoch in range(epochs): sampler.set_epoch(epoch) # ← different shuffle each epoch for step, (x, y) in enumerate(loader): with model.no_sync() if (step + 1) % accum else nullcontext(): with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16): loss = criterion(model(x.cuda()), y.cuda()) / accum loss.backward() if (step + 1) % accum == 0: torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0) optimizer.step() optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True) ``` **Four details that determine whether you get 1.9× or 7.1×:** - **`no_sync()`** on all but the final microstep. This was the Pune fix — without it you all-reduce once per microbatch instead of once per optimiser step. - **`sampler.set_epoch(epoch)`.** Forget it and every epoch sees the identical shuffle, which quietly degrades training. - **`bucket_cap_mb`** controls how gradients are grouped for overlapped communication. DDP starts the all-reduce for early buckets while later layers are still computing backward. Too small and you get overhead; too large and you lose overlap. - **`gradient_as_bucket_view=True`** avoids a full extra copy of the gradients. **Memory per GPU under DDP** is the full model plus gradients plus optimiser state — nothing is saved. DDP buys speed, not capacity. ```bash torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 --nnodes=1 train.py ``` ##### ZeRO and FSDP The insight behind ZeRO (Rajbhandari et al., 2020): under DDP, every GPU stores identical copies of gradients and optimiser state. That is pure redundancy. Shard them instead. | Stage | Shards | Memory per GPU (Ψ params, N GPUs) | Extra comms | |---|---|---|---| | DDP | Nothing | `2Ψ + 2Ψ + 12Ψ` | All-reduce | | **ZeRO-1** | Optimizer state | `2Ψ + 2Ψ + 12Ψ/N` | Same as DDP | | **ZeRO-2** | + gradients | `2Ψ + 2Ψ/N + 12Ψ/N` | Reduce-scatter | | **ZeRO-3** | + parameters | `(2Ψ + 2Ψ + 12Ψ)/N` | + all-gather (1.5× DDP) | ```python def zero_memory(params_B, n_gpus, stage=3, dtype_bytes=2): P = params_B * 1e9 weights, grads, optim = P * dtype_bytes, P * dtype_bytes, P * 12 # fp32 Adam + master if stage >= 1: optim /= n_gpus if stage >= 2: grads /= n_gpus if stage >= 3: weights /= n_gpus return round((weights + grads + optim) / 1e9, 1) for stage in [0, 1, 2, 3]: print(f"7B, 8 GPUs, ZeRO-{stage}: {zero_memory(7, 8, stage):>6.1f} GB/GPU") # ZeRO-0: 112.0 ZeRO-1: 38.5 ZeRO-2: 36.8 ZeRO-3: 14.0 ``` **ZeRO-3 turns a model that needs 112 GB into one that needs 14 GB per GPU.** That is the difference between impossible and routine. The mechanism: during the forward pass, each GPU all-gathers the parameters for the layer it is about to compute, uses them, and immediately frees them. Same in reverse for backward. You trade communication for memory. **FSDP** is PyTorch's native implementation of the same idea: ```python import functools from torch.distributed.fsdp import ( FullyShardedDataParallel as FSDP, MixedPrecision, ShardingStrategy, CPUOffload, StateDictType, FullStateDictConfig, ) from torch.distributed.fsdp.wrap import transformer_auto_wrap_policy mp_policy = MixedPrecision( param_dtype=torch.bfloat16, reduce_dtype=torch.float32, # ← reduce in fp32 for stability buffer_dtype=torch.bfloat16, ) auto_wrap = functools.partial( transformer_auto_wrap_policy, transformer_layer_cls={TransformerBlock}, # wrap per block ) model = FSDP( model, auto_wrap_policy=auto_wrap, mixed_precision=mp_policy, sharding_strategy=ShardingStrategy.FULL_SHARD, # = ZeRO-3 device_id=torch.cuda.current_device(), limit_all_gathers=True, use_orig_params=True, # needed for torch.compile and param groups ) model.gradient_checkpointing_enable() ``` **`transformer_auto_wrap_policy` is the setting people get wrong.** Wrapping the whole model as one FSDP unit means all-gathering every parameter at once — no memory saving at all. Wrapping per transformer block means you hold one block's parameters at a time. Always specify the layer class. **`reduce_dtype=torch.float32`** matters for stability. Gradient reduction in bf16 accumulates error across ranks; fp32 reduction costs bandwidth and prevents a class of subtle divergence. Checkpointing under FSDP needs care, since parameters are sharded: ```python save_policy = FullStateDictConfig(offload_to_cpu=True, rank0_only=True) with FSDP.state_dict_type(model, StateDictType.FULL_STATE_DICT, save_policy): state = model.state_dict() if rank == 0: torch.save(state, "checkpoint.pt") ``` For very large models, use `SHARDED_STATE_DICT` instead — each rank writes its own shard, avoiding a full gather onto rank 0. ##### DeepSpeed Same ZeRO stages, configured through JSON, plus CPU and NVMe offloading. ```json { "bf16": {"enabled": true}, "zero_optimization": { "stage": 3, "offload_optimizer": {"device": "cpu", "pin_memory": true}, "offload_param": {"device": "cpu", "pin_memory": true}, "overlap_comm": true, "contiguous_gradients": true, "reduce_bucket_size": 5e8, "stage3_prefetch_bucket_size": 5e8, "stage3_param_persistence_threshold": 1e6, "stage3_gather_16bit_weights_on_model_save": true }, "gradient_accumulation_steps": 8, "gradient_clipping": 1.0, "train_micro_batch_size_per_gpu": 4, "steps_per_print": 50 } ``` **CPU offloading is the escape hatch** when even ZeRO-3 does not fit. Optimiser state moves to host RAM, and the CPU performs the Adam update. It is roughly 2–4× slower per step, and it lets you fine-tune a 70B model on 8×A100-40GB — which would otherwise be impossible. `FSDP` and `DeepSpeed` are largely interchangeable for ZeRO-3. FSDP is native and integrates better with `torch.compile`; DeepSpeed has more mature offloading and a larger set of tuning knobs. ##### Tensor and pipeline parallelism **Tensor parallelism** splits individual weight matrices across GPUs. In an MLP, the up-projection is split column-wise and the down-projection row-wise, so exactly one all-reduce is needed per block. ```python # Conceptual: Megatron-style MLP tensor parallelism # W_up (d, 4d) split column-wise → each rank holds (d, 4d/N) # W_down (4d, d) split row-wise → each rank holds (4d/N, d) # # forward: y_local = act(x @ W_up_local) @ W_down_local # y = all_reduce(y_local) ← one collective per block ``` **Tensor parallelism requires very fast interconnect.** Every block triggers an all-reduce of the full activation tensor, so it is viable within a node over NVLink and generally not across nodes over Ethernet. The standard configuration is TP degree = GPUs per node, typically 8. **Pipeline parallelism** assigns contiguous layer groups to different GPUs and streams microbatches through. Communication is point-to-point activations, which is far cheaper than all-reduce — so it works across nodes. Its problem is the **bubble**: while GPU 0 processes microbatch 1, GPUs 1–7 are idle. Interleaved schedules (1F1B) shrink the bubble to roughly `(P−1)/M` where `P` is pipeline stages and `M` is microbatches. Use at least 4× as many microbatches as stages. **3D parallelism** combines all three, and is how frontier models are trained: ```python def parallelism_plan(total_gpus, gpus_per_node=8, model_B=70, seq_len=8192): tp = min(gpus_per_node, 8) # within a node, NVLink remaining = total_gpus // tp pp = 4 if model_B > 30 else 1 # across nodes dp = remaining // pp return {"tensor_parallel": tp, "pipeline_parallel": pp, "data_parallel": dp, "total": tp * pp * dp} print(parallelism_plan(512)) # {'tensor_parallel': 8, 'pipeline_parallel': 4, # 'data_parallel': 16, 'total': 512} ``` ##### Gradient checkpointing Orthogonal to parallelism, and often the highest-return single flag. Instead of storing every activation for the backward pass, store only layer boundaries and **recompute** the rest. Memory drops from O(L) to roughly O(√L); compute rises about 30%. ```python from torch.utils.checkpoint import checkpoint class Block(nn.Module): def forward(self, x): if self.gradient_checkpointing and self.training: return checkpoint(self._forward, x, use_reentrant=False) return self._forward(x) ``` **`use_reentrant=False`** is the modern variant and is required for compatibility with FSDP and `torch.compile`. **Selective checkpointing** is better still — recompute the cheap operations (norms, activations) and keep the expensive ones (attention outputs, matmuls). Roughly 90% of the memory saving for 10% of the compute cost. ##### Measuring what matters ```python import time import torch.distributed as dist class ScalingProfiler: def __init__(self, model_params, world_size, seq_len, micro_bs, accum): self.n = model_params self.world = world_size self.tokens_per_step = seq_len * micro_bs * accum * world_size def step(self, dt, gpu_peak_tflops=312, mfu_target=0.40): tps = self.tokens_per_step / dt flops = 6 * self.n * tps mfu = flops / (gpu_peak_tflops * 1e12 * self.world) return {"tokens_per_sec": int(tps), "tokens_per_sec_per_gpu": int(tps / self.world), "mfu": round(mfu, 3), "step_time_s": round(dt, 3), "healthy": mfu >= mfu_target * 0.8} ``` **Scaling efficiency** is the number to report: `throughput(N GPUs) / (N × throughput(1 GPU))`. Above 0.85 is good; the Pune team's 1.9/8 = 0.24 was a red flag that should have been caught on day one. **Diagnosing poor scaling:** | Symptom | Likely cause | Fix | |---|---|---| | High all-reduce time | Microbatch too small | Raise microbatch, use `no_sync` | | MFU < 0.2 | Data loader starving GPUs | More workers, `pin_memory`, prefetch | | Uneven rank times | Stragglers, imbalanced data | Check `drop_last`, node health | | OOM at higher DP | Activation memory | Gradient checkpointing | | Slow FSDP | Wrong wrap policy | Wrap per transformer block | Profile with `torch.profiler` and look at the NCCL kernel time as a fraction of the step. ##### Common mistakes - **No `no_sync()` with gradient accumulation** — the 1.9× disaster. - **Forgetting `sampler.set_epoch()`**, reusing the same shuffle every epoch. - **FSDP without an auto-wrap policy**, gathering the whole model at once. - **`reduce_dtype=bf16`** in FSDP mixed precision, accumulating reduction error. - **Tensor parallelism across nodes** over Ethernet. - **Too few microbatches** for pipeline parallelism, so the bubble dominates. - **Not measuring scaling efficiency** and assuming N GPUs means N× throughput. - **Gradient checkpointing everywhere** when selective would cost less compute. - **`use_reentrant=True`** (the old default) breaking FSDP compatibility. - **Saving a FULL_STATE_DICT** for a very large model, OOMing rank 0. - **Blaming the GPUs** when the data loader is the bottleneck. ##### Hands-on: measure the scaling curve Your practical task converts a single-GPU script to FSDP or DeepSpeed and measures throughput scaling. Run on 1, 2, 4, and 8 GPUs and plot tokens/second against GPU count with an ideal-linear reference line. Then profile the 8-GPU run and report the fraction of step time in NCCL collectives. That fraction is the single number that explains your scaling efficiency. The mini project fine-tunes a model too large for one GPU using ZeRO-3 with offloading. Document the memory and speed trade-off explicitly: peak VRAM per GPU and step time for ZeRO-2, ZeRO-3, and ZeRO-3 with CPU offload. The expected pattern — each stage buying memory at a throughput cost — is the trade-off you will be asked to reason about in any infrastructure interview. The assignment is a guide on when to use each strategy, with memory calculations. Build a decision tree keyed on model size, GPU memory, interconnect, and node count, and include the `zero_memory` function so a reader can compute their own case. Add a worked example for a 70B fine-tune on 8×A100-80GB, showing why ZeRO-3 with selective checkpointing is the answer and what the alternatives cost. ##### Key takeaways - **Distributed training is bounded by communication, not compute.** Measure scaling efficiency, and treat anything below 0.85 as a bug to diagnose. - **DDP replicates and buys speed; ZeRO/FSDP shards and buys capacity** — ZeRO-3 takes a 7B model from 112 GB per GPU to 14 GB. - **`no_sync()` during gradient accumulation and a per-block FSDP wrap policy** are the two settings that most often separate working from broken. - **Tensor parallelism needs NVLink and stays within a node; pipeline parallelism tolerates slow links but needs many microbatches** to hide the bubble. - **Gradient checkpointing is the cheapest memory lever** — roughly √L activation memory for 30% more compute, and selective checkpointing gets most of it for far less.
practical_task_reference: Convert a single-GPU training script to multi-GPU using FSDP or DeepSpeed and measure throughput scaling.
mini_project_reference: Fine-tune a model that does not fit on one GPU using ZeRO-3 offloading and document memory and speed tradeoffs.
